Welcome toOscillator & Reservoir

One oscillator shares quanta with a reservoir — how likely is each level?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: the level probabilities of one oscillator, from counting reservoir microstates

Source

Concept
One oscillator (levels Ei = iε, one microstate each) shares q = uNR quanta (u = q/NR is the quanta per reservoir oscillator) with a reservoir of NR oscillators. Every microstate of the isolated pair is equally likely, so pi = ΩR(q − i) / Σj ΩR(q − j), with ΩR(n) = (n + NR − 1)! / [n! (NR − 1)!], counted exactly through ln Γ.
Serves
Explain why each level's probability is proportional to the reservoir's multiplicity, and how that relates to the Boltzmann factor e−Ei/kBT.
On screen
Upper chart: exact pi for levels 0–20 on a fixed log axis 10−8–1 (grey ▼ = below 10−8, grey × = level above q). Lower chart: pi+1/pi = (q − i)/(q − i + NR − 1). The dashed curve, when switched on, is xi/Z with x = q/(q + NR − 1) and Z = 1/(1 − x), summed over all levels (at NR = 1, where the one-oscillator reservoir has no single T and the formula gives x = 1, it is drawn flat at 1/(q + 1)). Temperatures appear as kBT/ε = 1/ln[(q + NR − 1)/q]; zero-point energy is omitted because it cancels.
Inquiry
Five questions, each answered by setting NR, u and the comparison switch and reading the charts and the Readouts panel, then a closing summary of where the Boltzmann factor comes from.
Misconception
Alternative intuitions appear only as answer choices and are addressed in feedback after a choice is made.

Pedagogy principles applied

Commit, then checkEach question is a gated choice; the student commits, then checks against the charts.
Operational quantitiesProbabilities come from an exact count of reservoir microstates; readouts are the ratios and temperature the questions name, to 3 dp.
Stable scalesAxes are fixed (levels 0–20, 10−8–1, ratio 0–1), so any change of shape is a change of physics.
Controlled variableu = q/NR is held while NR changes, keeping the reservoir's energy per oscillator fixed.
Staged revealsThe dashed comparison curve is drawn only when switched on; rows of the sidebar Readouts panel appear when a question uses them.
Formal layer on demandDerivations live in The Physics sheet, not on the charts.
One Oscillator and a Reservoir
Probability of each level of the small oscillator (log scale)
Ratio of neighbouring probabilities

Guided Inquiry

1 · Sharing with one oscillator

Set u = 2 and the reservoir size to NR = 1, so that the small oscillator shares q = 2 quanta with one other oscillator. How do the probabilities of the levels compare?

2 · A reservoir of two

Keep u = 2 and set NR = 2, so that q = 4, and look at the plot and at p1/p0, which reads 0.800. Why is level 0 now the most likely level of the small system?

3 · Growing the reservoir

Keep u = 2 and set NR = 10, where p1/p0 reads 0.690 and p11/p10 reads 0.526. Step the reservoir size up through 20, 50 and 100 to 1000, watching the lower chart and these two readouts. What happens to the ratio of neighbouring probabilities?

4 · A small reservoir against the curve

Keep u = 2 with NR back at 10, and switch on the comparison curve: the Boltzmann factor at this reservoir's temperature. How do the exact points for the small reservoir compare with the dashed curve?

5 · What sets the slope

Keep NR = 1000 and the comparison curve on, and set u to 1, then 2, then 3, reading kBT/ε and p1/p0 each time. What sets how steeply the line falls?

6 · Where the Boltzmann factor comes from

The probability of each level of the small oscillator is proportional to the number of microstates the reservoir has left: pi ∝ ΩR(q − i). Each quantum the oscillator takes divides that count by a factor set by the reservoir's temperature.

For a large reservoir that factor is the same for every quantum, e−ε/kBT, so pi ∝ e−Ei/kBT: the Boltzmann factor. A small reservoir cools as it gives up energy, so its high levels fall below the Boltzmann line.

One Oscillator and a Reservoir

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

One small oscillator shares a fixed number of energy quanta with a reservoir of other oscillators, and every arrangement of the pair is equally likely. The sim counts the arrangements and plots how likely each level of the small oscillator is.

What you'll learn

  • Why the probability of a level comes from counting the reservoir's microstates.
  • How the ratio of neighbouring probabilities depends on the size of the reservoir.
  • How this count is related to the Boltzmann factor.
  • What controls the slope of the points on the log plot.
The apparatus: one oscillator, a reservoir, and a fixed total of quanta.

What's on screen

  • Upper chart, blue dots: the exact probability pi of each level i = 0 to 20, on a log axis from 10−8 to 1. A grey × marks a level above q, which cannot be reached; a grey ▼ marks one below 10−8.
  • Amber dashed curve (switch on Comparison curve): the Boltzmann factor e−Ei/kBT/Z at the reservoir's temperature.
  • Lower chart: the ratio pi+1/pi for each level, from 0 to 1. With the curve on, an amber dashed line marks e−ε/kBT.
  • Readouts: NR, q, kBT/ε, p1/p0 and p11/p10.
See itDraw the charts for your current settings. Watch for: the blue dots for your reservoir size and u, and the readouts matching them.

Both charts have fixed axes: levels 0–20, probability 10−8–1, ratio 0–1. A change of shape is therefore a change of physics.

03

A level's probability is the number of ways the reservoir can hold the rest

The small oscillator has levels Ei = iε, one microstate each. With the reservoir it holds q = u NR quanta, and the pair is isolated. Every microstate of the pair is equally likely, so level i has probability in proportion to the number of ways the reservoir can hold the other q − i quanta (notes §4.4):

pi = ΩR(q − i) / Σj ΩR(q − j)

ΩR(n) = (n + NR − 1)! / [ n! (NR − 1)! ]

Notes (4.41), with the Einstein-solid count (5.37). The notes write 3N for the number of oscillators; here it is NR.

Taking one more quantum from the reservoir multiplies its count by a simple factor, and the lower chart plots it:

pi+1/pi = ΩR(q − i − 1)/ΩR(q − i) = (q − i) / (q − i + NR − 1)

It is zero once level i holds all q quanta.

At the opening, NR = 10 and u = 2, so q = 20. Then p1/p0 = 20/29 = 0.690 and p11/p10 = 10/19 = 0.526, the two ratios in the Readouts.

See itSet NR = 10 and u = 2, with the curve off. Watch for: p1/p0 reading 0.690 and p11/p10 reading 0.526, the values the two fractions give.
04

Small reservoirs: one oscillator makes the levels equally likely, two make level 0 the most likely

With NR = 1 and u = 2 the pair holds q = 2. One oscillator holds whatever is left in exactly one way, ΩR = 1, so levels 0, 1 and 2 each have probability 1/3. Levels above 2 cannot be reached, and kBT/ε reads “no single T”.

ΩR(q − i), the number of ways the reservoir holds what level i leaves, for NR = 1 and NR = 2 at u = 2.

With NR = 2 and u = 2 the pair holds q = 4. Two oscillators hold n quanta in n + 1 ways, so levels 0 to 4 have 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 ways out of 15. Level 0 is the most likely, at 1/3, and p1/p0 = 4/5 = 0.800.

Level 0 wins here because leaving all the quanta with the reservoir gives it the most arrangements, not because the small oscillator seeks low energy. With one reservoir oscillator nothing favours it.

See itSet NR = 1 and u = 2. Watch for: levels 0, 1 and 2 at the same height, grey × marks from level 3, and p1/p0 reading 1.000.
See itSet NR = 2 and u = 2. Watch for: five dots falling from 1/3 at level 0 to 1/15 at level 4, and p1/p0 reading 0.800.
05

As the reservoir grows, the neighbouring ratios draw together

A larger reservoir feels the loss of a quantum less. At u = 2, p1/p0 goes 0.690, 0.678, 0.671, 0.669, 0.667 for NR = 10, 20, 50, 100, 1000, while p11/p10 goes 0.526, 0.612, 0.647, 0.657, 0.666.

The two ratios against reservoir size at u = 2. They meet at u/(u + 1).

When NR is large, q = u NR is large too, and taking ten quanta out of it hardly changes (q − i)/(q − i + NR − 1). Every ratio then tends to u/(u + 1), which is 2/3 at u = 2. The points on the log plot fall by the same factor at each step, so they lie on a straight line.

See itSet NR = 1000 and u = 2, with the curve off. Watch for: p1/p0 reading 0.667 and p11/p10 reading 0.666, and the blue dots on one straight line.
06

The Boltzmann factor is the large-reservoir limit; a small reservoir falls below it

Notes §4.4 expands ln ΩR(Etot − Ei) in Ei (eq 4.42). The first term falls by Ei/kBT, giving pi ∝ e−Ei/kBT (4.43). The next term is smaller by about Ei/(T CR), and it vanishes only for a reservoir whose temperature does not change as it gives up energy.

NR = 10, u = 2. The exact points against the comparison curve, at kBT/ε = 2.691.

At NR = 10 and u = 2 the points lie within about 0.03 of the curve, in log10, over levels 0–4. Then they fall below it: by 0.05 at level 5, 0.39 at level 10 and 3.74 at level 20. Ten oscillators with 20 quanta cool as they are drained, so each further quantum divides the count by a larger factor.

A wrong normalisation would shift every point by the same amount. Here the low levels agree and the high ones do not, so the gap is the cooling of a small reservoir. At NR = 1000 the gap at level 20 is only 0.014.

See itSet NR = 10 and u = 2, with the curve on. Watch for: blue dots on the dashed curve for the first few levels, then falling away: level 20 near 10⁻⁷.⁵, the curve near 10⁻³.⁷.
See itSet NR = 1000 and u = 2, with the curve on. Watch for: the blue dots sitting on the dashed curve all the way to level 20.
07

The slope is set by the reservoir's temperature, not by its size

The sim reads the temperature from the reservoir's own count, using the exact finite-difference form of notes (5.40):

kBT/ε = 1/ln[ΩR(q)/ΩR(q − 1)] = 1/ln[(q + NR − 1)/q]

Exact one-quantum difference. Notes (5.40), kBT/ε = 1/ln[(q + NR)/q] with ε for the notes’ ℏω, is its large-NR (Stirling) form.

Comparing with the first ratio, p1/p0 = ΩR(q − 1)/ΩR(q) = e−ε/kBT: one quantum taken costs the reservoir that factor in microstates. For a large reservoir the same factor applies at every level.

The exact points at NR = 1000 for u = 1, 2 and 3. Each set lies on a straight line.

At NR = 1000, u = 1, 2, 3 give kBT/ε = 1.444, 2.468, 3.479 and p1/p0 = 0.500, 0.667, 0.750. A reservoir with more quanta per oscillator is hotter and loses a smaller share of its microstates per quantum, so the line is flatter: it falls by 0.301, 0.176 and 0.125 in log10 per level.

See itSet NR = 1000, u = 1, with the curve on. Watch for: kBT/ε reading 1.444, p1/p0 reading 0.500, and the steepest line.
See itSet NR = 1000, u = 3, with the curve on. Watch for: kBT/ε reading 3.479, p1/p0 reading 0.750, and the flattest line.
08

Where it matters

  • Any small system in a heat bath. The same argument gives pi = e−βEi/Z, with β = 1/kBT (notes 4.43–4.44). The Maxwell speed distribution of §1.2 rests on this factor, which the notes assumed there and derive here.
  • Temperature from counting. The reservoir is an Einstein solid (notes §5.4). Its temperature is the rate at which ln Ω grows with energy, the quantity the sim reads out.
Go deeper: why the notes expand ln Ω

ΩR varies enormously with energy; at NR = 10 and u = 2 it runs from 1 at level 20 to 10 015 005 at level 0. Its logarithm varies slowly enough to expand (notes 4.42).

09

Summary

In one line. The sim shares q quanta between one oscillator and a reservoir, counts the reservoir's microstates for each level of the oscillator, and plots the exact probabilities against the Boltzmann factor.

Key points

  • pi ∝ ΩR(q − i): a level is as likely as the reservoir has ways to hold the rest.
  • The ratio (q − i)/(q − i + NR − 1) falls with i; for a large reservoir it is the same at every level, u/(u + 1).
  • Then pi ∝ e−Ei/kBT. A small reservoir cools as it gives up energy and its high levels fall below that line.
  • The slope is set by the reservoir's temperature: p1/p0 = e−ε/kBT.

Common mix-ups

  • “Level 0 is the most likely because the small system seeks low energy.” At NR = 1 the three reachable levels are equal, 1/3 each.
  • “With u fixed, the ratios stay put as NR grows.” At u = 2 they move from 0.690 and 0.526 at NR = 10 to 0.667 and 0.666 at 1000.
  • “A richer reservoir makes the line steeper.” Raising u from 1 to 3 at NR = 1000 raises p1/p0 from 0.500 to 0.750: the line is flatter.

Things to try on your own

  • Work out p1/p0 for NR = 5 and u = 2 from q/(q + NR − 1), then check the readout.
  • Predict p1/p0 for NR = 20 and u = 3, then check.
